grammar.title: Grammar
grammar.rule: ここに｜ふだが｜あります。ここに｜ゆいが｜います。

tables.caption: Objects and people in the chapter

grammar.note_en:
あります states that an inanimate thing is present; います states that a person or animal is present. ここにゆいがいます means “Yui is here.” つくえのうえにほんがあります means “There is a book on the desk.” に marks the place, and が marks the person or thing whose presence you are introducing. These are polite nonpast forms. This chapter does not teach their negative or past paradigms.

A known topic can come first with は: ゆいのほんはつくえのうえにあります, “Yui’s book is on the desk.” You are locating that known book, rather than introducing the fact that a book exists. Do not assume は and が can be exchanged mechanically in every sentence. れんはつくえのとなりにいます means “Ren is next to the desk.” Physical objects use あります even if someone owns them; people use います even if they are standing still.

うえ is the space above or on something; した is below or under it. の links the reference object to this position: つくえのうえ, “on the desk”; いすのした, “under the chair.” Add に to mark that phrase as a place for the existence verb. なか is inside, となり is next to, and うしろ is behind. The pictures and changing arrangements distinguish them; do not translate every English in/on/at with the same Japanese noun.

ここ is the place close to the speaker, そこ is close to the listener or already indicated, and あそこ is away from both. Their reference follows the speaker, rather than being permanent names for parts of the room. In this chapter Yui first indicates the desk near Ren and then the shelf farther away. どこ asks where. めいさんはどこですか, “Where is Mei?”, uses です with a place question; めいさんはどこにいますか is the fuller existence question. Use あります when the located entity is an object.

も means also or too. れんもいます means “Ren is here too.” With a location, にも combines place marking with also: たなのとなりにもかばんがあります, “There is a bag next to the shelf too.” In れんのほんもあります, “Ren’s book is here too,” も replaces the が used to introduce the existence of that book. This is the chapter’s bounded addition pattern, not a rule that も always replaces the immediately preceding particle.

わたし means I/me. わたしのふだ is “my tag”: it identifies the speaker, so Mei’s and Yui’s わたし refer to different people. はい is yes in the affirmative identification exchange here. Speakers continue to use さん for another person’s name, and omit it from their own name. The large loose card belonging to Yui is different from Mei’s small tag on the umbrella. At the end Mei’s recovered tag lies next to the open envelope, whose interior is visibly empty; the story’s last question remains unanswered.

Keep both parts of a spatial relation when answering: ふうとうのとなりにあります, “It is next to the envelope.” A bare word such as となり can be a conversational fragment, but C asks for your own complete sentence or full predicate. The visible stage cues tell you which arrangement to recall. Charts and exact word meanings for this chapter remain in How to read; all typed answers use taught kana spellings.
